Developing a Musical Mind; Series 3 When Musical Thinking Meets Performance There is a major difference between knowing music and responding musically. The rehearsal room gives us time to prepare but the stage gives us reality. Something may go wrong. A singer may enter late. A musician may miss a chord. The sound system may behave differently from rehearsal. The audience may respond unexpectedly. A performer may suddenly feel nervous. Another section of the choir may become too loud. The tempo may move too fast or slow. A microphone may fail. In such moments, technical ability is important—but musical awareness becomes even more important. “The real test of a musical mind is not only how well you perform when everything goes according to plan, but how intelligently you respond when it doesn’t.” — Victor Adenola Performance Requires Listening One of the biggest mistakes performers make is becoming so focused on themselves that they stop listening. A singer may be thinking – Am I singing well? A pianist may be thinking – Am I playing correctly? A conductor may be thinking – Am I giving the right gestures? These questions have their place, but performance requires something larger: What is happening musically right now? The singer must hear the accompaniment. The instrumentalist must hear the other musicians. The choir must listen to one another. The conductor must listen to the entire ensemble. The band must listen to the vocalist and the musical direction. Performance is a conversation. My Experience as a Music Director One experience that has remained particularly memorable for me happened when my wife and I were expecting our first child. She went into labour on the same day my choir had a concert. My wife was experiencing labour pains, while members of the choir were excited about the concert and waiting for me to conduct the songs. It was an emotionally demanding situation. It reminded me that leadership in music does not happen in a vacuum. Musicians are human beings, and real life continues even when there is a performance scheduled. A music director must therefore develop more than conducting technique. You need judgement. You need emotional awareness. You need the ability to assess a situation quickly. You need to understand what the music needs—and sometimes, what the people involved need. That experience reinforced something I have come to appreciate deeply in music leadership: Musical intelligence must be accompanied by human intelligence. Musical Thinking Creates Flexibility A musician who only memorises instructions may struggle when circumstances change. But a musician who understands the music can adapt. If the tempo changes, they can adjust. If the singer needs more space, they can respond. If the choir is struggling with balance, the director can make an adjustment. If the congregation responds differently from what was expected, a worship team can adapt without losing musical direction. This is why I encourage musicians to understand principles, not just instructions. Don’t only know what to play or sing. Understand why and how. What is the musical reason for the softer dynamic? What is different about this repetition? The Musical Mind and Expression Expression is not simply adding emotion to music. Expression comes from understanding. A performer should know where the music is going. Where does the phrase begin? Where does it peak? Where does it relax? What words deserve emphasis? Where should there be space? What should remain restrained? What should become more intense? When these decisions are intentional, expression becomes convincing rather than artificial. “Expression begins when a performer stops asking, ‘How do I feel today?’ and starts asking, ‘What does this music need me to communicate?’ — Victor Adenola This is particularly important for singers. Your personal emotions may change from day to day, but the musical responsibility remains. You may feel tired but still need to communicate confidence. You may feel nervous but still need to communicate calmness. You may feel joyful but the music may require restraint. Professional musicians learn to serve the music rather than becoming controlled entirely by their momentary emotions. The Musical Mind in a Choir A choir with a musical mind doesn’t simply sing its individual parts. Sopranos listen to altos. Altos listen to tenors. Tenors listen to basses. Everyone listens to the accompaniment. Everyone watches the conductor. Everyone understands the musical structure. The result is more than four vocal sections singing simultaneously. It becomes an ensemble. This principle applies equally to bands. A good band is not made up of musicians trying to prove how much they can play. It is made up of musicians who understand when to play, when to support, when to lead and when to leave space. From Performer to a Complete Musician Developing a musical mind changes your identity as a musician. You stop asking only: “Can I perform this?” You begin asking: “Do I understand this?” Then: “Can I communicate this?” And eventually: “Can I respond intelligently when circumstances change?” That is a much higher level of musicianship. A Challenge for Musicians At your next rehearsal or performance, don’t focus only on getting the notes right. Choose one additional goals: Listen more carefully. Observe the harmony. Pay attention to phrasing. Watch the conductor. Listen to another section. Notice the dynamics. Identify musical patterns. Respond rather than react. Think about what the music is communicating. Then ask yourself afterwards: What did I hear today that I would not have noticed a year ago? Your answer may reveal how much your musical mind is developing. Final Thought Musicianship is not simply the ability to reproduce music. It is the ability to understand, interpret, communicate and respond. The hands may play the instrument. The voice may produce the sound. The eyes may read the score. But the musical mind connects everything together. “When the ear, mind, technique and expression work together, the musician does more than perform music—the musician communicates it.” — Victor Adenola That is the goal of musical development. Not merely to produce sound.
